source.title: Double Descent Demystified: Identifying, Interpreting & Ablating the Sources of a Deep Learning Puzzle
source.authors: Rylan Schaeffer; Mikail Khona; Zachary Robertson; Akhilan Boopathy; Kateryna Pistunova; Jason W. Rocks; I. Fiete; O. Koyejo

record.tranche_reason: The study tests double descent through polynomial and ordinary linear regression, rather than reproducing the original deep-network experiments.
record.gate_note: The study reports test-error curves and ablations of three proposed causes. It also discusses cited findings about nonlinear autoencoders and other work; those cited results are not recorded as rows. Its singular-value plots are mechanistic evidence, not measurements of a version's named outcome.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own test-error sweeps. It sweeps P in polynomial regression and N in ordinary linear regression on synthetic and three tabular datasets. It also runs causal ablations that remove the peak. These are different methods aimed at whether double descent occurs and what drives it.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors identify three factors that together produce double descent in linear regression: small non-zero training singular values, test-feature variation along those modes, and residual errors of the best model projecting onto them. Ablating any one prevents it on synthetic and three real datasets. They also argue the residuals need not be random noise and that the intuition extends to nonlinear models via feature maps and infinite-width limits.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses polynomial and ordinary linear regression, including data-size sweeps and causal ablations, rather than deep-network model-size or epoch sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The presence of double descent changes when small singular values are removed, test features are restricted to the training-feature subspace, or residual prediction errors are eliminated.

fits_no_version.finding: The smallest non-zero singular value of the training features reaches its minimum at N=P on all three real datasets (right panels of Figs. 3, 5, 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The double-descent peak coincides with a minimum of the smallest non-zero training-feature singular value at the interpolation threshold.

record.problems: Reported curve values are shown in figures without numerical extraction in the text. No uncertainty estimates are stated. The real datasets were randomly selected for accessibility, and the experiments are limited to regression settings.
record.rows_left_out: No additional directly relevant test-error outcomes were left out. The singular-value plots in Figures 3, 5, and 6 were omitted because they measure a proposed mechanism rather than the test-error behavior named by the versions.

untested.parts: No deep networks; the polynomial P sweep is not a deep-network model-size sweep.
Only ordinary linear regression; no deep networks.
Only polynomial regression in a capacity sweep; other model classes (kernels, trees, networks) are not tested.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested across axes.
No multiple or triple peaks. No optimally tuned ridge (ridge is only discussed). No graded label-noise manipulation.

record.verdict_notes: This is a tutorial-style paper, and all curves are figure only with no uncertainty. The record says code is 'not stated', but the text says code is publicly available. The ablation rows' state 'absent' describes double descent itself; for V6 links, that absence matches the version's prediction. V4 links to the N-sweep rows were removed because V4 names a capacity axis; a reviewer accepting the authors' P/N-ratio equivalence could restore them. The polynomial target has no stated noise, which hints at a peak without label noise, but the text does not say so explicitly. The reader's guess linking the V3 and V4 limits_scope to the ablations is retained for V3 only.

versions.untested_parts: The polynomial-regression illustration varies feature count, but the study does not test model-wise double descent in deep networks.
No test-error sweep over training epochs or time.
The study varies training-set size in linear regression; it does not test this effect in deep networks.
Tests are limited to polynomial regression and ordinary linear regression, not a broad set of model classes.
The study proposes interacting factors and discusses singular values, but does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.

Tests removal of residual errors, but does not test multiple peaks or optimally tuned regularization. It does not separately manipulate random label noise; the discussion says random noise is not necessary.
No re-counting of parameters or demonstration that the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

relationships.reason: Based on the text (Sec. 4 and 7), not a separate experiment. The authors argue residuals can be fully deterministic misspecification, so random label noise is unnecessary. The zero-residual ablations (r8, r11, r14, r17) remove both kinds together.
relationships.display_finding: The authors argued that deterministic misspecification could generate peak-driving residuals, while zero-residual ablations jointly removed deterministic and noisy contributions.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Sections 4 and 7 allow deterministic residuals, but Section 4 explicitly identifies their amplified contribution as variance. V6 already permits variance without label noise, so this argument supports that mechanism rather than limiting the stated version; r8,r11,r14,r17 do not isolate residual sources.

relation.reason: The study reports its own double-descent results and interventions that eliminate the effect.

tranche.reason: Own polynomial-capacity sweeps, linear-regression sample sweeps and causal ablations test double descent using a different method from the deep-network sweeps described in the pack.

source_check.notes: Ablation-row states describe absence of double descent, consistent with support for its removal under V6. The code=n metadata conflicts with the abstract and Section 5, which state that code is publicly available.

statements.correction: Section 4: residuals may be random or deterministic; the residual-dependent term is identified as variance and causes double descent. Section 6: replacing targets with full-dataset linear predictions eliminates the peak. Section 7: random noise is unnecessary. These facts qualify a label-noise-necessity claim and support V6's variance mechanism.
statements.problem: The study-specific facts are correct, but the limits_scope placement does not follow for V6 as written: V6 already allows variance rather than label noise.
